nameStory: This beetle gets its "longhorn" name from its impressively long antennae that can stretch as long as or longer than its entire body - like having antennae that reach from your head to your toes! The "round-necked" part refers to the cylindrical shape of its thorax (the middle body section), which distinguishes it from other longhorn beetles with flattened or angular necks.
description: The Round-necked Longhorn Beetle is a medium-sized wood-boring beetle with distinctively long, thread-like antennae that give the entire longhorn beetle family its name. These beetles typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a somewhat cylindrical body shape. Adults are often brown to black in color with lighter markings or bands across their wing covers. Like all longhorn beetles, they have strong mandibles (jaws) and spend much of their larval stage tunneling through dead or dying wood.

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thread-like and extend at least as long as the body, often longer - they feel delicate and segmented if gently touched

idTips.label: Cylindrical thorax
idTips.description: The middle body section behind the head is rounded and tube-like rather than flattened, giving it a distinctly "round-necked" appearance

idTips.label: Body size
idTips.description: Medium-sized beetle, roughly the length of your thumbnail, with a somewhat elongated oval shape

idTips.label: Wing cover patterns
idTips.description: Hard wing covers often show lighter bands or markings against a darker background, creating subtle striped patterns

idTips.label: Strong jaws
idTips.description: Prominent mandibles that look capable of chewing through wood - you can see them extending forward from the head

habitat: Look for Round-necked Longhorn Beetles in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, particularly where there are dead or dying trees. They're often found on or near fallen logs, dead branches, and standing dead trees (called snags) where they lay their eggs. Adults may be spotted on flowers feeding on pollen and nectar, especially on wildflowers in forest clearings and edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their woody homes as temperatures warm, often found on early blooming flowers like wild cherry or serviceberry.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen feeding on flowers during the day and searching for mates. This is the best time to spot them.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases as they focus on mating and egg-laying in dead wood. Look for small, round exit holes in dead branches.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae are actively tunneling inside dead wood, creating the sawdust-like frass you might notice at the base of dead trees.

funFact: Longhorn beetle larvae can spend up to three years secretly tunneling through a single piece of dead wood, creating elaborate mazes of galleries that can completely hollow out a branch - sometimes the only sign of their presence is a small pile of sawdust at the base of the tree and the eventual emergence of dozens of adults through perfectly round exit holes!
confusionNotes: Round-necked Longhorn Beetles are most easily confused with other longhorn beetle species, but the cylindrical (round) thorax is the key distinguishing feature - many other longhorns have flattened or more angular thoraxes. Remember: "round-necked" means the middle section looks like a tube, not a pancake.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their wood-boring reputation, longhorn beetles are actually beneficial to forest ecosystems as adults are important pollinators, and their larvae help decompose dead wood, recycling nutrients back into the soil. They're only considered pests when they attack living trees or wooden structures.
compareHints: Since this is the only Clytus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other longhorn beetles by focusing on the round, cylindrical thorax rather than the flattened or square thorax of most other species. The combination of medium size, long antennae, and that distinctive tube-like middle section sets it apart from the dozens of other longhorn species in our region.
